reason: The sources provide more than 10 highly consistent, cross-verified claims to tell a surprising story about the Sombrero Galaxy's dual nature and violent merger history.
story: For centuries, the Sombrero Galaxy (M104) was beloved as a serene, hat-shaped marvel floating 28 to 31 million light-years away in Virgo. But advanced space telescopes have unmasked a terrifying truth: this cosmic beauty is actually a freakish hybrid built on galactic cannibalism. By peering through its thick dust ring, Spitzer and James Webb revealed that the Sombrero is two galaxies stuffed into one. Its flat, spinning disk is nested inside a gargantuan elliptical galaxy's halo. Its inner core is warped like a giant funnel—a permanent scar from ancient, violent mergers where it devoured smaller neighbor galaxies. At the heart of this cosmic graveyard lies an even darker secret: a dormant supermassive black hole weighing up to a billion suns. The Sombrero's tranquil exterior is nothing but a mask for a history of pure cosmic violence.
angle: The Sombrero Galaxy is actually two galaxies stuffed inside one, featuring a warped core scarred by a violent history of galactic cannibalism.

claims.claim: The Sombrero Galaxy is also known as Messier 104 (M104) and NGC 4594.
It was discovered on May 11, 1781, by French astronomer Pierre Méchain.
Although discovered in 1781, it was not officially added to the Messier Catalogue until 1921.
The Sombrero Galaxy is located in the constellation Virgo.
The galaxy is estimated to be approximately 28 to 31 million light-years away from Earth.
From our perspective on Earth, the galaxy is viewed nearly edge-on.
Its most prominent visual feature is a dark, symmetrical dust lane (or ring) that encircles its bright central bulge.
The galaxy has a total mass estimated to be equivalent to 800 billion suns.
It contains a massive population of globular clusters, estimated to number around 2,000.
At the center of the galaxy lies a supermassive black hole.
This central black hole is estimated to have a mass of approximately 1 billion solar masses.
Spitzer Space Telescope observations revealed that the galaxy's halo is much larger and more massive than previously thought, characteristic of a giant elliptical galaxy.
Astronomers describe the galaxy as having a dual nature, acting like 'two galaxies, one inside the other' because it combines a flat disk inside a massive elliptical halo.
The galaxy possesses a violent history of cosmic collisions and mergers, meaning it has grown through galactic cannibalism.

disputed: Whether the dust ring is a major site of star formation: older sources (S1, S2) say yes, but JWST observations (S7) show surprisingly few young stars, suggesting it is not. The script should explain this shift in scientific understanding.
The galaxy's physical diameter: S1 cites roughly 95,000 to 105,000 light-years, while S4 cites 50,000 light-years. The script should leave out exact size measurements to avoid confusion.

The exact distance to the galaxy: S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, and S6 suggest slightly different distances ranging from 28 to 31 million light-years. The script should describe it broadly as 28 to 31 million light-years away.

The exact mass of the central black hole: S1 and S5 mention 1 billion solar masses, but S1 also notes a 2016 study finding 6.4 hundred million solar masses. The script should state it is around 640 million to 1 billion solar masses.
